publicTrace: PolicyEngine API returned an error (status: error); the calibration fallback is carrying this run with widened uncertainty per the uncertainty multiplier (1.4x applied to CI half-width).

Base rate / reference class: CBO and JCT scores of fully refundable $3,000 CTC proposals in 2021-2023 ranged from roughly $80B to $130B per year for a single tax year, with the American Rescue Plan's expanded CTC costing ~$120B/year and more targeted proposals landing lower. The calibrated point estimate of $109.6B sits near the center of this reference class.

Mechanism: A $3,000 fully refundable CTC replaces the current $2,000 partially refundable credit. The incremental cost comes from (a) the $1,000 per-child increase for taxpayers already receiving the full $2,000, (b) the refundability extension reaching lower-income families currently excluded by the earned-income phase-in, and (c) removal of the $1,400 refundability cap. The calibration prior applies a 1.04 multiplier and $3.5B additive to account for take-up, timing, and behavioral differences between static microsimulation and official scoring.

Disconfirming consideration (outcome below $78.8B): If current law already includes a more generous baseline (e.g., TCJA extensions partially enacted), or if child population counts are lower than modeled, the true cost could fall well below the interval.

Disconfirming consideration (outcome above $140.4B): If behavioral responses (e.g., reduced labor supply among secondary earners) are larger than assumed, or if take-up of the refundable portion is higher than historical rates, official scores could exceed $140B.

Calibration note: Because the PolicyEngine API errored, the uncertainty multiplier of 1.4 was applied to the minimum CI half-width of $22B, yielding an effective half-width of ~$30.8B, reflected in the 80% interval of [$78.8B, $140.4B]. The distribution is right-skewed to reflect asymmetric upside risk from full refundability.
The CDF support was set to [$50B, $180B] to cover tail scenarios including partial legislative implementation or scoring methodology differences.
assumptions: Current law baseline is pre-TCJA-extension, meaning the $2,000 CTC with partial refundability (up to $1,600 in 2026 under current law) is the starting point.
The reform applies to tax year 2026 only (single-year cost), not a multi-year window.
Child population and income distribution follow CBO's January 2025 baseline projections.
Take-up of the newly refundable portion is assumed at 85% of eligible families, consistent with EITC historical take-up rates.
No behavioral labor supply response is modeled in the point estimate; behavioral effects are captured in the uncertainty widening.
dataCaveats: PolicyEngine API returned an error; no raw model output is available. The calibrated point estimate of $109.6B is derived entirely from the calibration prior and reference class, not from a live microsimulation run.

The calibration prior (rawToFinalRatio=1.04, additive=$3.5B) was developed by comparing PolicyEngine static scores to official JCT/CBO scores on prior CTC proposals; it may not transfer perfectly to this specific reform design.
The 'current law' baseline for 2026 is uncertain pending Congressional action on TCJA extensions, which could materially shift the incremental cost of this reform.
Nominal dollar figures are not inflation-adjusted; if the forecast is evaluated against a real-dollar official score, a small discrepancy may arise.
drivers: Refundability extension to lowest-income families (largest cost driver)
Per-child credit increase from $2,000 to $3,000 for middle/upper-middle income families
Number of qualifying children under age 17 in 2026
Income phase-in and phase-out structure relative to current law
Take-up rate among newly eligible low-income families
